content: Chronic plaque psoriasis is the most prevalent form of psoriasis, characterized by red, thickened, and scaly skin lesions. The first-line treatment for this condition typically involves topical therapies, which include vitamin D analogues, corticosteroids, tar-based preparations, dithranol, salicylic acid, and topical retinoids. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness, tolerability, and safety of these topical treatments compared to placebo, as well as to compare vitamin D analogues (used alone or in combination) with other topical therapies. The review included a comprehensive search of multiple databases up to February 2011, with additional searches for adverse effects conducted in February 2011 and August 2012. Although the final searches identified additional studies, these were not incorporated into the current review but will be included in future updates. The review focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared active topical treatments against placebo or vitamin D analogues in individuals with chronic plaque psoriasis. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed by one author and verified by another, with additional data on adverse events and withdrawals collected. This update added 48 new trials, bringing the total to 177 RCTs involving 34,808 participants. These included 26 trials on scalp psoriasis and 6 trials on inverse or facial psoriasis. The analysis revealed that most vitamin D analogues were significantly more effective than placebo when applied to the body. For example, twice-daily becocalcidiol showed a standardized mean difference (SMD) of -0.67, while once-daily paricalcitol had an SMD of -1.66. These results correspond to improvements of 0.8 and 1.9 points, respectively, on a 6-point global improvement scale. Corticosteroids also demonstrated superior efficacy compared to placebo. Potent corticosteroids had an SMD of -0.89, translating to a 1.0-point improvement, while very potent corticosteroids had an SMD of -1.56, equating to a 1.8-point improvement. Other treatments, such as dithranol, combined vitamin D/corticosteroid therapy, and tazarotene, also outperformed placebo. However, head-to-head comparisons between vitamin D analogues and corticosteroids yielded mixed results. For both body and scalp psoriasis, combined vitamin D and corticosteroid therapy was more effective than either treatment alone. Vitamin D analogues generally outperformed coal tar but showed variable results compared to dithranol. For scalp psoriasis, vitamin D analogues were less effective than both potent and very potent corticosteroids. Indirect evidence from placebo-controlled trials supported these findings. Potent corticosteroids were less likely than vitamin D analogues to cause local adverse events, such as burning or irritation. Combined vitamin D/corticosteroid therapy was as well-tolerated as potent corticosteroids and better tolerated than vitamin D analogues alone. Only 25 trials assessed dermal atrophy, and while few cases were reported, the methods used to evaluate this adverse effect were not robust. Clinical assessments of dermal atrophy are generally insensitive and detect only severe cases. No significant differences in systemic adverse effects were observed between topical agents. In conclusion, corticosteroids are at least as effective as vitamin D analogues and are associated with fewer local adverse events. However, there is insufficient evidence regarding the risk of dermal atrophy with long-term corticosteroid use. Further research is needed to guide long-term maintenance therapy and provide comprehensive safety data.
